arguments.heading: Argument analysis: March 30, 2026 session
paragraphs: This session was the only argument held. No reargument occurred, so nothing here covers a later session. The analysis below covers each side and the questions tested.

The the side that brought the case asked the Court to hold the Section 1519 offense was committed in San Francisco. His reasoning: the crime completes upon falsification, with intent coinciding at that moment. No communication, effect, or investigation is required. He cited Travis, Armour Packing, and Johnson.

He argued Lamar required a communicative assertion, comparing it to Palliser. He said venue is count-specific and waivable, using a Cabrales analogy. He noted the government's own trial position placed falsification on the defendant's computer. He agreed Section 1512(c) differs because it requires effects.

The government asked the Court to uphold trial where the investigation was actually affected. Its reasoning: the transmission targeted that district, like shooting and hitting it. It cited Ford and Lamar for detrimental effects supporting venue.

It conceded the elements were complete before transmission and effects are not elements. It argued Cabrales is backward-looking while Section 1519 is forward-looking. It distinguished Johnson as a mere mailing case. It said venue requires action producing the effect. If the investigation's location were unknown, venue would follow the act's location.

In rebuttal, the government reiterated that the venue-related effect is not an element. It said its theory requires both intent and an actual effect in the other district. In the shredding hypothetical, it said venue would have to be in Seattle. It also said a pure essential-conduct test would favor the the side that brought the case.

Justice Thomas tested whether saving a draft completes the crime. The the side that brought the case answered yes, saving with the required intent completes it. Justice Sotomayor tested proof of intent without sending. Justice Kavanaugh tested whether intent to impede must be shown.

Justice Alito tested where the crime happens if material is emailed to San Francisco. Justice Kavanaugh probed the shredding-at-home example and challenged the actual-effect requirement as absent from the statutory text. Justice Kagan asked how the theory differs from the lower court's. Justice Sotomayor questioned who decides the extra-textual intent requirement.
No reargument session appears in the approved record. Nothing can be said about changes after reargument.

case.dek: The Court heard argument on where a federal fraud crime counts as happening.

dek_sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 1, lines 1-9

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case asks where a federal fraud crime counts as happening. The dispute centers on a law called Section 1519. The question is whether the crime was committed in San Francisco. The answer decides where a trial can take place.
Section 1519 punishes someone who creates a false record to hide something. The parties disagree about when that crime is complete. They also disagree about where it happens.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 4, lines 23-25

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The approved record shows the case reached the Supreme Court as No. 25-5146. The Court held oral argument on March 30, 2026, in Washington, D.C. The record does not describe the lower court's decisions, so this summary cannot cover them.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 1, lines 1-9

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The the side that brought the case, represented by Tobias S. Loss-Eaton, asks the Court to hold the crime happened in San Francisco. He argues the crime was complete when the false record was created, with no sending or effect required.

The government, represented by Anthony A. Yang, asks the Court to allow trial where the investigation was actually affected. It says the sending targeted another district, like a shot aimed at a target.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The the side that brought the case says Section 1519 is complete upon falsification. He says intent must coincide with that falsification. He says duplicates are not separate falsifications and no metadata evidence was shown. He cites older cases supporting a location tied to the physical act.

The government concedes the crime's elements were complete before any transmission. It concedes effects are not elements. It concedes that without transmission, venue would follow where the act occurred. But it argues the sending here actually affected the investigation district. It cites cases about detrimental effects supporting venue.

Justice Alito asked where the crime happens if the material is emailed to San Francisco. Justice Kagan asked how the government's theory differs from the lower court's approach. Justice Sotomayor questioned who decides the extra-textual intent requirement the government proposes.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: Venue rules decide where a person faces trial. That choice affects convenience, local juries, and prosecution strategy. The ruling could shape how courts locate crimes committed on computers. It may also clarify whether effects on investigations can anchor a trial.

paragraphs: The Court has not announced its decision. The approved record shows only that argument was held. The parties await the Court's judgment.
